m1-4-q1.s: The command history keeps the commands you recently typed in a buffer, so you can **recall** them with the Up arrow (or Ctrl+P) instead of retyping. The buffer holds **10** lines by default, and you can **change its size**.
x: The buffer is cleared when you log out, so commands from a previous session are gone.
The default is 10 lines, not 15.
History stays in memory; it is not written to a log file.

m1-4-q2.s: Power on → the switch first runs **POST** (power-on self-test), which checks the CPU, DRAM and flash. Only after POST passes does it load the boot loader.
x: Boot loader, CPU initialization and loading IOS all come after POST.

m1-4-q3.s: Password recovery needs **physical (console) access**: you connect to the console port, interrupt the boot, and bypass the startup configuration. It cannot be done remotely.

m1-4-q4.s: `login local` tells a line (console or VTY) to check the **local username database**. That database must have at least one entry, so you also need `username ... secret ...`.

m1-4-q5.s: Use **show controllers** to see the auto-MDIX setting of a specific interface (the full form includes the PHY keyword).
code: Switch# show controllers ethernet-controller fa0/1 phy
x: show interfaces shows status, errors and counters, not the MDIX setting.

m1-4-q6.s: In a duplex mismatch, the **full-duplex** side transmits whenever it wants, so the **half-duplex** side keeps detecting collisions after it has already started sending. These are **late collisions**, and they show up on the half-duplex end.
x: Full-duplex ports do not use CSMA/CD, so they never count collisions.
Serial interfaces are not Ethernet.

m1-4-q7.s: The **BOOT environment variable** says where the IOS image is. You set it with `boot system`.
x: config-register and confreg set the configuration register (a router feature), not the image path.

m1-4-q8.s: The boot loader reads the **BOOT environment variable** to find and load the IOS image. If the variable is not set, it searches flash for the first usable image.

m1-4-q9.s: **SSH** encrypts the whole remote session, including passwords. That makes it the secure replacement for Telnet.
x: FTP, HTTP and POP send data in plain text.
NetBEUI is an old, non-routable LAN protocol.

m1-4-q10.s: A loopback is a **logical (software) interface inside the router**. It is up as long as the router is running and has no physical port.
x: It needs no `no shutdown`.
You can create many loopbacks.
It cannot be cabled to another device.

m1-4-q11.s: The minimum valid Ethernet frame is **64 bytes**. Anything smaller is a **runt** (usually a collision fragment) and is dropped. The maximum standard frame is 1518 bytes, which carries 1500 bytes of data.

m1-4-q12.s: Boot order: 1) **POST**, 2) load the **boot loader**, 3) low-level CPU initialization, 4) initialize the flash file system, 5) load IOS. So the boot loader runs right **after POST**.

m1-4-q13.s: A Layer 2 switch forwards broadcasts out every port, so adding one makes the **broadcast domain bigger**. At the same time, each switch port is its own collision domain, so collision domains get *smaller* and more numerous.
x: Switches reduce collisions; they don't add them.
Collision domains shrink; they don't grow.

m1-4-q14.s: **Cut-through** switching starts forwarding as soon as it has read the destination MAC address. It never checks the FCS, so frames are forwarded **without error checking**. That gives low latency.
x: Fragment-free is the variant that checks the first 64 bytes.
Buffering for mixed speeds is a store-and-forward feature.

m1-4-q15.s: A **hub** repeats bits out every port, so everything attached shares **one collision domain**. A **switch** makes **each port its own collision domain**. Both still forward broadcasts everywhere, so neither one splits broadcast domains.

m1-4-q16.s: A switch forwards a frame by looking up the **destination MAC address in its MAC (CAM) table**, which maps MAC addresses to ports.
x: Cut-through can forward bad frames, because it does not check the FCS.
Unknown unicasts are flooded too, not just broadcasts.
A frame is filtered (dropped) if its destination is on the same port it arrived on.

m1-4-q17.s: Buffers **store frames temporarily** when a port is busy, for example when traffic from a fast port has to leave through a slower one. This stops frames from being dropped during congestion.

m1-4-q18.s: **High port density** means more devices connect to the same switch. More traffic stays local instead of crossing uplinks between switches, which relieves congestion.

m1-4-q19.s: **ASICs** (application-specific integrated circuits) do the forwarding in hardware. That cuts the time each frame spends inside the switch.

m1-4-q20.s: Frame processing order: 1) Check whether the **source MAC** is in the table, and add it with the incoming port if it isn't. 2) Look up the **destination MAC**. 3) If it is known, forward out that port; if it is unknown, **flood** it out every port except the one it arrived on.

m1-4-q21.s: Switches **learn** by recording the **source MAC address and the port the frame came in on**. They use the *destination* MAC only to decide where to forward the frame.
x: Layer 2 switches do not look at IP addresses when building the MAC table.

m1-4-q22.s: **Store-and-forward** receives the whole frame and checks its **FCS (CRC)**. Only error-free frames are forwarded.
x: Cut-through does no error checking; fragment-free checks only the first 64 bytes.
FCS is a field in the frame, not a switching method.

m1-4-q23.s: Routers stop broadcasts, so **every router interface is the edge of a broadcast domain**. In the exhibit there are 4 LANs plus 4 router-to-router links: **4 + 4 = 8** broadcast domains.

m1-4-q24.s: Turn DTP off (`switchport nonegotiate`, with a manual trunk or access mode) on **links that should never trunk** and on **links to non-Cisco switches**, because DTP is Cisco-proprietary.

m1-4-q25.s: On an 802.1Q trunk, frames in the **native VLAN are sent untagged**. Both ends must agree on the same native VLAN, so it acts as a **common identifier** for that untagged traffic. Best practice is to use an unused VLAN for it, not VLAN 1.
x: User traffic belongs in data VLANs, and voice in the voice VLAN.
Remote management uses the management VLAN.

m1-4-q26.s: `no vlan 100` in global configuration mode deletes just that one VLAN.
x: `delete flash:vlan.dat` wipes **all** VLANs.
The two interface commands only change port membership; VLAN 100 still exists.

m1-4-q27.s: `show vlan brief` lists only **access ports**. **Trunk ports** don't belong to a single VLAN, so they are left out. Use `show interfaces trunk` to see them.

m1-4-q28.s: A VLAN is a **broadcast domain**. A broadcast from VLAN 20 reaches **only VLAN 20 devices**, even across trunks to other switches.

m1-4-q29.s: The exhibit shows that VLAN 20 isn't in the trunk's allowed list, so VLAN 20 frames never cross it. Add it to the allowed list.
code: SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 20
x: DTP is already negotiating, so enabling it changes nothing.
Moving the PCs to the default or native VLAN breaks the intended design.

m1-4-q30.s: When a VLAN is deleted, its ports **stay assigned to the missing VLAN** and become **inactive**. They can't communicate until you recreate the VLAN or assign the ports to another one. They do **not** fall back to VLAN 1.

m1-4-q31.s:
The 802.1Q tag is 4 bytes:
**Type (TPID)** – 2 bytes, value 0x8100, marks the frame as tagged.
**User priority (PCP)** – 3 bits for CoS/QoS.
**CFI** – 1 bit (originally for Token Ring).
**VLAN ID (VID)** – 12 bits, so up to 4096 IDs.

m1-4-q32.s: The router has to route between several VLANs over one link (router-on-a-stick), so the switch port facing it must be a **trunk**.

m1-4-q33.s:
DTP modes:
**dynamic auto** – becomes a trunk only if the neighbor is trunk or desirable (passive).
**dynamic desirable** – actively asks to become a trunk.
**trunk** – always a trunk, and still sends DTP.
**nonegotiate** – stops sending DTP frames.

m1-4-q34.s: Removing the access VLAN sends the port **back to VLAN 1** (the default). VLAN 30 itself is not deleted, and the port stays up.

m1-4-q35.s: `show interfaces <id> switchport` shows a port's VLAN settings: administrative and operational mode, trunk encapsulation, access VLAN, native VLAN and voice VLAN.

m1-4-q36.s: A voice VLAN is assigned with **switchport voice vlan**, not switchport access vlan. A port can have one access (data) VLAN **and** one voice VLAN.

m1-4-q37.s: Voice VLAN setup: **create the voice VLAN**, put the port in **access mode**, **trust the CoS** marking from the phone, and **assign the voice VLAN** to the port.
x: The phone port is an access port, not a trunk, and no subinterfaces are needed.

m1-4-q38.s: `show interfaces trunk` lists only interfaces that are trunking. **G0/2 is missing**, so it isn't configured as a trunk, and VLAN traffic toward Server 1 can't cross it.

m1-4-q39.s: On a router subinterface, you have to set the VLAN tag with **encapsulation dot1Q** *before* IOS accepts an IP address. That's why the error appears.

m1-4-q40.s: Routers don't negotiate DTP, so the switch port facing a router-on-a-stick must be set as a trunk manually.
x: dynamic desirable relies on DTP replies, which the router never sends.

m1-4-q41.s: Router-on-a-stick uses **one router interface split into subinterfaces**, one per VLAN. That requires the switch port connecting to the router to be a **trunk**.
x: A multilayer switch is a different method (SVIs).
Needing one router port per VLAN is the legacy method.

m1-4-q42.s: Router-on-a-stick needs a **dedicated router**, and all VLANs share **one physical link**. With many VLANs that link becomes a bottleneck. A multilayer switch routes in hardware between SVIs instead.
x: SVIs belong to the multilayer-switch method.
Each subinterface uses a different subnet, and only one physical interface is needed.

m1-4-q43.s: In **legacy** inter-VLAN routing each router port connects to a switch **access port in that VLAN**. Gi1/1 is a **trunk** and is in the **default VLAN**. It should be an access port in VLAN 10.

m1-4-q44.s: The subinterface for VLAN 10 is tagging with the **wrong VLAN**: `encapsulation dot1Q 5`. The number after dot1Q must match the VLAN the hosts are in.
x: The physical interface needs no IP address when you use subinterfaces.
Subinterfaces come up with the physical interface; they need no separate `no shutdown`.

m1-4-q45.s: The router carries several VLANs on one link, so the switch side must be a **trunk port**.
x: An SVI is used when a multilayer switch does the routing.
A routed port is a Layer 3 port on a multilayer switch.

m1-4-q46.s: Each subinterface needs an IP in **the same subnet as the hosts in its VLAN**. Here the addresses are swapped between subinterfaces, so every host's gateway sits in the wrong subnet.

m1-4-q47.s: G0/0.30 has an IP address outside **172.16.30.0/24**, so VLAN 30 hosts can't reach their default gateway.
x: The physical interface doesn't need an IP.
Subinterfaces don't need `no shutdown`.

m1-4-q48.s: A **routed port** (`no switchport`) acts like a router interface: it **isn't part of any VLAN**, it doesn't trunk, and it takes an IP address directly.

m1-4-q49.s: The PC, printer, IP phone and switch management address are each in a **different subnet/VLAN**. One subinterface per VLAN means **4 subinterfaces**.

m1-4-q50.s: `mdix auto` turns on automatic crossover detection. The port swaps its transmit and receive pairs as needed, so **either a straight-through or a crossover cable** works.

m1-4-q51.s: On a Layer 2 switch the IPv4 address goes on the **SVI** (for example, interface vlan 1). That address is used for remote management.

m1-4-q52.s: `configure terminal` moves you from privileged EXEC mode (`#`) into **global configuration mode** (`(config)#`).

m1-4-q53.s: `configure terminal` moves you from privileged EXEC mode into **global configuration mode**.
x: Saving the configuration is `copy running-config startup-config`.
Disabling an interface is `shutdown`.

m1-4-q54.s: `shutdown` **administratively disables** the interface you're configuring, whether it is physical or an SVI. `no shutdown` turns it back on.

m1-4-q55.s: `shutdown` puts the interface in the **administratively down** state, so it stops passing traffic until you enter `no shutdown`.

m1-4-q56.s: On a 2960 the IPv6 address goes on the **SVI**, which is the switch's virtual management interface.

m1-4-q57.s: `exit` goes **up one level**: from interface mode back to **global configuration mode**. (`end` or Ctrl+Z jumps straight to privileged EXEC mode.)

m1-4-q58.s: `enable` moves you from user EXEC mode (`>`) to **privileged EXEC mode** (`#`).

m1-4-q59.s: **Full duplex** means the port sends and receives **at the same time**, with no collisions. Half duplex sends in only one direction at a time.

m1-4-q60.s: A **data (user) VLAN** carries ordinary user traffic. Voice and management traffic should each have their own VLAN, for QoS and security.

m1-4-q62.s: A **voice VLAN** separates IP-phone traffic so QoS can prioritize it and give calls the bandwidth they need.

m1-4-q63.s: Out of the box, **VLAN 1, the default VLAN**, is also the native VLAN and the **management VLAN** (interface vlan 1). Best practice is to move management to a dedicated VLAN.

m1-4-q64.s: Voice traffic needs low delay, so the target is **under 150 ms one way**. A **voice VLAN** with QoS helps meet it.

m1-4-q65.s: **Data VLANs** split users and devices into logical groups, such as by department, each in its own broadcast domain.

m1-4-q66.s: The **management VLAN** carries traffic used to manage devices remotely: SSH, Telnet, HTTP/HTTPS and SNMP. The switch's management SVI lives in this VLAN.

m1-4-q68.s: On an 802.1Q trunk, frames in the **native VLAN** are sent **untagged**. A switch that receives an untagged frame puts it in its own native VLAN.

m1-4-q69.s: Only the **native VLAN** travels **untagged** across an 802.1Q trunk. Every other VLAN gets a tag.

m1-4-q70.s: Router interfaces are **administratively down by default**. Enable the interface with `no shutdown`.

m1-4-q71.s: `transport input all` allows both Telnet and SSH. To allow **SSH only**, change it on the VTY lines.

m1-4-q72.s: Each switch port is its own collision domain (microsegmentation). A **high port density switch** gives every device its own port, which practically eliminates collisions.
x: Routers and firewalls separate networks; they don't fix collisions inside a LAN.

m1-4-q73.s: With **SVIs on a multilayer switch**, routing is done in hardware, so it's **fast**, and **no separate router** is needed.
x: Subinterfaces belong to router-on-a-stick.
Hosts still need a default gateway (the SVI's IP address).
EtherChannel bundles physical ports, not SVIs.

m1-4-q74.s: In `encapsulation dot1q ?` the missing value is the **VLAN number** whose tagged frames this subinterface handles.

m1-4-q75.s: The **native VLAN** is the one sent **untagged** on an 802.1Q trunk. Best practice is to use an unused VLAN for it.

m1-4-q76.s: `show vlan brief` lists each VLAN with its name, status and **access ports**, so you can see which VLAN every switch port belongs to.
x: MAC-to-port mappings come from `show mac address-table`.
Trunk and native-VLAN details come from `show interfaces trunk`.

m1-4-q77.s: In the activity, SW1's Gi0/1 (toward the router) isn't a trunk, so inter-VLAN routing fails. After you make it a trunk, PC1 reaches the server and the page shows **File Server**.

m1-4-q78.s:
DHCPv4 messages in order (DORA):
**DHCPDISCOVER** – the client looks for a server (broadcast).
**DHCPOFFER** – the server offers an address.
**DHCPREQUEST** – the client accepts the offer.
**DHCPACK** – the server confirms the lease.

m1-4-q79.s: The **management VLAN** is for traffic that manages devices: SSH, Telnet, HTTP/HTTPS and SNMP. Keeping it separate from user data improves security.
